exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field Using Linearity Properties

question.text: Calculate $\nabla \cdot (\mathbf{F}-5\mathbf{G})$ for the vector fields $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf G,$ where \[ \mathbf{F}=\left(x^2+y^2 \right)\,\mathbf{i}+xy \,\mathbf{j}, \quad \nabla \cdot \mathbf{G}=x-y. \]
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for divergence:

  • $\nabla \cdot (k \mathbf F) = k \nabla \cdot \mathbf F$

  • $\nabla \cdot (\mathbf F + \mathbf G) = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F + \nabla \cdot \mathbf G.$

In our case, we have

\begin{align*} \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{F}-5\mathbf{G}) &=\nabla\cdot \mathbf{F}-\nabla\cdot (5\mathbf{G})\\[5pt] &=\nabla\cdot \mathbf{F}-5\nabla\cdot \mathbf{G}. \end{align*}

First, we need to calculate $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}.$ In doing so, we get \begin{align*} \nabla \cdot \mathbf F &=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(x^2+y^2 \right)+\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(xy)\\[5pt] &=2x+x\\[5pt] &=3x. \end{align*}

Applying the linearity properties, we get

\begin{align*} \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{F}-5\mathbf{G}) &=\nabla\cdot \mathbf{F}-5\nabla\cdot \mathbf{G}\\[5pt] &= 3x - 5\cdot \left(x-y\right)\\[5pt] &= 3x - 5x+5y\\[5pt] &= 5y - 2x. \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate $\nabla \cdot (3\mathbf{F}+2\mathbf{G})$ for the vector fields $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf G,$ where \[ \mathbf{F}=e^{\sin x}\,\mathbf{i}+\cos \left(y^2\right)\,\mathbf{j}, \quad \nabla \cdot \mathbf{G}=3y\sin\left(y^2\right). \]
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for divergence:

  • $\nabla \cdot (k \mathbf F) = k \nabla \cdot \mathbf F$

  • $\nabla \cdot (\mathbf F + \mathbf G) = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F + \nabla \cdot \mathbf G.$

In our case, we have

\begin{align*} \nabla \cdot (3\mathbf{F}+2\mathbf{G}) &=\nabla\cdot (3\mathbf{F})+\nabla\cdot (2\mathbf{G})\\[5pt] &=3\nabla\cdot \mathbf{F}+2\nabla\cdot \mathbf{G}. \end{align*}

First, we need to calculate $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}.$ In doing so, we get \begin{align*} \nabla \cdot \mathbf F &=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(e^{\sin x}\right)+\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\cos \left(y^2\right)\right)\\[5pt] &=\cos x e^{\sin x}-2y\sin \left(y^2\right). \end{align*}

Applying the linearity properties, we get

\begin{align*} \nabla \cdot (3\mathbf{F}+2\mathbf{G}) &=3\nabla\cdot \mathbf{F}+2\nabla\cdot \mathbf{G}\\[5pt] &= 3\left(\cos x e^{\sin x}-2y\sin \left(y^2\right) \right) + 2\cdot \left(3y\sin\left(y^2\right)\right)\\[5pt] &= 3\cos x \,e^{\sin x}-6y\sin \left(y^2\right) + 6y\sin\left(y^2\right)\\[5pt] &= 3\cos x \,e^{\sin x}. \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate $\nabla \cdot (\mathbf{F}-\mathbf{G})$ for the vector fields $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf G,$ where \[ \mathbf{F}=\ln{\left(xy^2\right)}\,\mathbf{i}-\dfrac 1y \,\mathbf{j}, \quad \nabla \cdot \mathbf{G}=\dfrac{1}{x}. \]
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for divergence:

  • $\nabla \cdot (k \mathbf F) = k \nabla \cdot \mathbf F$

  • $\nabla \cdot (\mathbf F + \mathbf G) = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F + \nabla \cdot \mathbf G.$

In our case, we have

\begin{align*} \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{F}-\mathbf{G}) &=\nabla\cdot \mathbf{F}+\nabla\cdot (-\mathbf{G})\\[5pt] &=\nabla\cdot \mathbf{F}-\nabla\cdot \mathbf{G}. \end{align*}

First, we need to calculate $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}.$ In doing so, we get \begin{align*} \nabla \cdot \mathbf F &=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\ln{\left(xy^2\right)}\right)+\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(-\dfrac 1y\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{y^2}{xy^2}+\dfrac{1}{y^2}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{y^2} . \end{align*}

Applying the linearity properties, we get

\begin{align*} \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{F}-\mathbf{G}) &=\nabla\cdot \mathbf{F}-\nabla\cdot \mathbf{G}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{y^2} -\dfrac{1}{x} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{y^2}. \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate $\nabla \cdot (-3\mathbf{F})$ for the vector field $\mathbf F$ where \[ \mathbf{F}=2x\cos x\,\mathbf{i}+2xy\sin x \,\mathbf{j}- 4z\,\mathbf{k}. \]
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for divergence:

  • $\nabla \cdot (k \mathbf F) = k \nabla \cdot \mathbf F$

  • $\nabla \cdot (\mathbf F + \mathbf G) = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F + \nabla \cdot \mathbf G.$

In our case, we have

\begin{align*} \nabla \cdot (-3\mathbf{F}) &=-3 \nabla\cdot \mathbf{F}. \end{align*}

First, we need to calculate $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}.$ In doing so, we get \begin{align*} \nabla \cdot \mathbf F &=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(2x\cos x)+\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(2xy\sin x )-\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}(4z)\\[5pt] &=2\cos x -2x\sin x+ 2x\sin x-4\\[5pt] &=2\cos x-4\\[5pt] &=2\left(\cos x-2\right) \end{align*}

Applying the linearity properties, we get

\begin{align*} \nabla \cdot (-3\mathbf{F}) &=-3 \nabla\cdot \mathbf{F}\\[5pt] &=-3 \cdot 2\left(\cos x-2\right)\\[5pt] &=6\left(2-\cos x\right). \end{align*}

question.text: Calculate $\nabla \cdot \left(-4\mathbf{F}\right)$ for the vector field $\mathbf F$ where \[ \mathbf{F}=x^2yz\,\mathbf{i} + (y^3 -y) \,\mathbf{j}- xyz^2\,\mathbf{k}. \]
question.explanation:
If $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf G$ are vector fields and $k$ is a constant, then we have the following linearity properties for divergence:

  • $\nabla \cdot (k \mathbf F) = k \nabla \cdot \mathbf F$

  • $\nabla \cdot (\mathbf F + \mathbf G) = \nabla \cdot \mathbf F + \nabla \cdot \mathbf G.$

In our case, we have

\begin{align*} \nabla \cdot \left(-4 \mathbf F\right) = -4 \nabla \cdot \mathbf F. \end{align*}

First, we need to calculate $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}.$ In doing so, we get \begin{align*} \nabla \cdot \mathbf F &=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2yz)+\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(y^3-y)+\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}(-xyz^2)\\[5pt] &=2xyz + 3y^2 -1 - 2xyz\\[5pt] &=3y^2-1. \end{align*}

Applying the linearity properties, we get

\begin{align*} \nabla \cdot \left(-4 \mathbf F\right) &= -4 \nabla \cdot \mathbf F\\[5pt] &= -4 \cdot \left(3y^2 -1\right)\\[5pt] &= 4 - 12y^2. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field Using the Product Rule

question.text: Given that $\mathbf F(x,y) = \langle \cos x, \sin y \rangle$ and $f(x,y) = \cos y + \sin x,$ calculate $\nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F).$
question.explanation:
We will use the following identity:

\[ \nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) = f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+ \mathbf F \cdot \nabla f \]

First, we compute $\nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}$ and $\nabla f.$ We get

\begin{align*} \nabla f &= \langle \cos x, -\sin y \rangle, \\[5pt] \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F} &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}(\cos x) + \dfrac{\partial }{\partial y}(\sin y)\\[5pt] &=-\sin x+\cos y\\[5pt] &=\cos y-\sin x. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \begin{align} \nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) &= f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+ \mathbf F \cdot \nabla f\\[5pt] &=(\cos y + \sin x)(\cos y-\sin x) + \langle \cos x, \sin y \rangle \cdot \langle \cos x, -\sin y \rangle\\[5pt] &=\cos^2 y - \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x-\sin^2 y\\[5pt] &=\left(\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x \right) +\left(\cos^2 y - \sin^2 y\right) \\[5pt] &=\cos 2x + \cos 2y. \end{align}

question.text: Given that $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle xy, zy, zx\rangle$ and $f(x,y,z) = xyz,$ calculate $\nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F).$
question.explanation:
We will use the following identity:

\[ \nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) = f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+ \mathbf F \cdot \nabla f \]

First, we compute $\nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}$ and $\nabla f.$ We get

\begin{align*} \nabla f &= \langle yz, xz, xy\rangle, \\[5pt] \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F} &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}(xy) + \dfrac{\partial }{\partial y}(zy)+ \dfrac{\partial }{\partial z}(zx) =y+z+x. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \begin{align} \nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) &= f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+ \mathbf F \cdot \nabla f\\[5pt] &=xyz(x+y+z) + \langle xy, zy, zx\rangle \cdot \langle yz, xz, xy\rangle\\[5pt] &=xyz(x+y+z) +xy^2z+xyz^2+x^2yz\\[5pt] &=xyz(x+y+z) +xyz(x+y+z) \\[5pt] &=2xyz(x+y+z). \end{align}

question.text: Given that $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle \ln{x}, xz^3, z^2\rangle$ and $f(x,y,z) = x^2z,$ calculate $\nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F).$
question.explanation:
We will use the following identity:

\[ \nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) = f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+ \mathbf F \cdot \nabla f \]

First, we compute $\nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}$ and $\nabla f.$ We get

\begin{align*} \nabla f &= \langle 2xz, 0, x^2\rangle, \\[5pt] \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F} &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}(\ln{x}) + \dfrac{\partial }{\partial y}(xz^3)+ \dfrac{\partial }{\partial z}(z^2) =\dfrac{1}{x}+ 2z. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \begin{align} \nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) &= f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+ \mathbf F \cdot \nabla f\\[5pt] &=x^2z\left(\dfrac{1}{x}+ 2z\right) + \langle \ln{x}, xz^3, z^2\rangle \cdot \langle 2xz, 0, x^2\rangle\\[5pt] &=xz +2x^2z^2 + 2xz\ln{x} +x^2z^2 \\[5pt] &=xz +3x^2z^2 + 2xz\ln{x} \\[5pt] &=xz(1+3xz + 2\ln{x}). \end{align}

question.text: Given that $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle y\ln z, z\ln x, x\ln y\rangle$ and $f(x,y,z) = x^2+2y^2+3z^2,$ calculate $\nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F).$
question.explanation:
We will use the following identity:

\[ \nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) = f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+ \mathbf F \cdot \nabla f \]

First, we compute $\nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}$ and $\nabla f.$ We get

\begin{align*} \nabla f &= \left\langle 2x, 4y, 6z \right\rangle, \\[5pt] \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F} &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}(y\ln z) + \dfrac{\partial }{\partial y}(z\ln x)+\dfrac{\partial }{\partial z}(x\ln y) =0 + 0 + 0=0. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \begin{align} \nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) &= f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+ \mathbf F \cdot \nabla f\\[5pt] &=\ln(x+2y+3z)\cdot 0+ \langle y\ln z, z\ln x, x\ln y\rangle \cdot \left\langle 2x, 4y, 6z \right\rangle\\[5pt] &=2xy\ln z+4yz\ln x+6xz\ln y . \end{align}

example.title: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field Using the Product Rule

question.text: Given that $\mathbf F(x,y) = \langle x, x^2y\rangle$ and $f(x,y) = xy,$ calculate $\nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F).$
question.explanation:
We will use the following identity:

\[ \nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) = f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+ \mathbf F \cdot \nabla f \]

First, we compute $\nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}$ and $\nabla f.$ We get

\begin{align*} \nabla f &= \langle y, x\rangle, \\[5pt] \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F} &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}(x) + \dfrac{\partial }{\partial y}(x^2 y) =1+x^2. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \begin{align} \nabla \cdot (f\,\mathbf F) &= f\, \nabla \cdot \mathbf {F}+ \mathbf F \cdot \nabla f\\[5pt] &=xy(1+x^2) + \langle x, x^2y\rangle \cdot \langle y, x\rangle\\[5pt] &=xy + x^3y + xy + x^3y\\[5pt] &=2xy + 2x^3y\\[5pt] &=2xy(1+x^2). \end{align}
